title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Blueprinty is a small software company that sells a specialized tool for engineering firms. Its software helps these firms draft the technical blueprints that accompany patent applications submitted to the United States Patent and Trademark Office. Like any vendor, Blueprinty would love to be able to tell prospective clients a simple, persuasive story: firms that use our software get more patents approved.
The cleanest way to support that claim would be to observe the same firms before and after adopting the software and watch their approval rates change. That experiment was never run, and no such longitudinal data exists. What Blueprinty does have is a cross-section of 1,500 mature (non-startup) engineering firms. For each firm we observe the number of patents awarded over the last five years, the region in which the firm operates, the firm’s age since incorporation, and whether the firm is a Blueprinty customer.
The trouble is that Blueprinty’s customers were not chosen at random. Firms decide for themselves whether to buy the software, and that decision is likely correlated with other things that also affect patent output — how established a firm is, where it is located, how aggressively it files. If customers happen to be older or concentrated in patent-heavy regions, a raw comparison of patent counts would credit the software for differences it did not cause. The rest of this post builds up a model that lets us compare customers and non-customers while holding firm age and region fixed, so that the customer effect is isolated as cleanly as observational data allows.

Firm age tells a similar story. Customers are, on average, a little older than non-customers. title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
The outcome we care about — patents awarded over five years — is a count. It cannot be negative and it cannot take fractional values like 2.7. A Normal distribution, which is continuous and unbounded in both directions, is a poor description of such data. The natural starting point for non-negative integer outcomes is the Poisson distribution, which places all of its probability mass on \(0, 1, 2, \dots\) and is fully described by a single rate parameter \(\lambda\) equal to both its mean and its variance.

Likelihood and log-likelihood
Suppose each firm’s patent count is an independent draw \(Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\) with probability mass function
\[
f(Y_i \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}.
\]
Because the firms are assumed independent and identically distributed, the joint likelihood of the whole sample is the product of the individual densities:
\[
L(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}
= \frac{e^{-n\lambda}\,\lambda^{\sum_i Y_i}}{\prod_i Y_i!}.
\]
Products of many small numbers are awkward to maximize, so we take logs. The log-likelihood turns the product into a sum:
\[
\ell(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big[ -\lambda + Y_i \log \lambda - \log(Y_i!) \Big]
= -n\lambda + \log(\lambda)\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(Y_i!).
\]
The last term does not involve \(\lambda\), so it does not affect where the maximum is — only the height of the curve.


Coding the log-likelihood

from scipy.special import gammaln  # log(Y!) = gammaln(Y + 1)

def poisson_loglikelihood(lmbda, Y):
    if lmbda <= 0:
        return -np.inf
    return np.sum(-lmbda + Y * np.log(lmbda) - gammaln(Y + 1))



Visualizing the log-likelihood
Using the observed patent counts as \(Y\), we can sweep \(\lambda\) across a grid and plot the resulting log-likelihood.





Poisson log-likelihood as a function of lambda, evaluated at the observed patent counts.




The curve is smooth, single-peaked, and concave. Reading the MLE off the plot is just a matter of finding the value of \(\lambda\) at the very top of the hill and dropping straight down to the horizontal axis — that location is the value of \(\lambda\) that makes the observed data most probable. The dashed line marks the sample mean, and the peak sits right on top of it.


Solving for the MLE analytically
We can confirm that algebraically. Differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to \(\lambda\):
\[
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = -n + \frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i.
\]
Setting the derivative to zero and solving:
\[
-n + \frac{\sum_i Y_i}{\lambda} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat{\lambda}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i = \bar{Y}.
\]
This “feels right”: the Poisson distribution’s mean is \(\lambda\), so the best single-number guess for the rate is simply the average count we observed.


Finding the MLE numerically
To check the algebra, we maximize the log-likelihood numerically by minimizing its negative.

neg_ll = lambda l: -poisson_loglikelihood(l[0], Y)
res = optimize.minimize(neg_ll, x0=[1.0], method="Nelder-Mead")

compare = pd.DataFrame({
    "Method": ["Numerical MLE (optimizer)", "Sample mean (closed form)"],
    "Estimate of lambda": [res.x[0], Y.mean()]
})
show(compare, {"Estimate of lambda": "{:.4f}"},
     "Numerical vs. closed-form MLE")






Table 4: Numerical vs. closed-form MLE

The two numbers agree to several decimal places. They should: the optimizer is searching for the top of exactly the same concave curve we differentiated by hand, and that peak is the sample mean. Any tiny discrepancy is just the optimizer’s convergence tolerance, not a real disagreement.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Poisson Regression
A single \(\lambda\) for every firm is too blunt. We saw that customers differ from non-customers in age and region, and those variables plausibly affect patenting on their own. The fix is to let each firm have its own rate parameter that depends on its characteristics:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \qquad \text{where} \qquad \lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta).
\]
Why the exponential? The rate \(\lambda_i\) must be strictly positive — a negative expected patent count is meaningless. But the linear index \(X_i'\beta\) can be any real number, positive or negative, depending on the covariates and coefficients. Wrapping it in \(\exp(\cdot)\) maps the whole real line onto the positive reals, guaranteeing a valid rate for every possible combination of inputs. It also makes the model multiplicative: a one-unit change in a covariate scales \(\lambda_i\) by a constant factor rather than adding a constant amount.

The regression log-likelihood
Substituting \(\lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)\) into the Poisson log-likelihood gives a function of the coefficient vector \(\beta\):
\[
\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big[ -e^{X_i'\beta} + Y_i (X_i'\beta) - \log(Y_i!) \Big].
\]

def poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X):
    eta = np.clip(X @ beta, -30, 30)   # clip to avoid overflow in exp
    lam = np.exp(eta)
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * eta - gammaln(Y + 1))

def neg_loglik(beta, Y, X):
    return -poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X)

def neg_score(beta, Y, X):
    # gradient of the negative log-likelihood: X'(lambda - Y)
    lam = np.exp(np.clip(X @ beta, -30, 30))
    return X.T @ (lam - Y)



Building the design matrix
The covariate matrix begins with a column of 1’s for the intercept, then firm age, then age squared, then binary indicators for the regions, and finally the customer indicator.
Two modeling choices deserve a word of explanation. First, age squared: the relationship between a firm’s age and its patent output is unlikely to be a straight line forever. Very young firms are still ramping up, and very old firms may plateau or decline; a quadratic term lets the model bend to capture that curvature instead of forcing a strictly linear trend. Second, we drop one region indicator. With an intercept already in the model, including a dummy for every region would make the region columns sum to the intercept column — perfect collinearity, which leaves the coefficients unidentified. Dropping one region (here, the Midwest) makes it the baseline; every other region’s coefficient is then read relative to the Midwest.

reg_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df["region"], prefix="region", drop_first=False)
reg_dummies = reg_dummies.drop(columns=["region_Midwest"]).astype(float)

X_df = pd.concat(
    [
        pd.Series(1.0, index=df.index, name="intercept"),
        df["age"].astype(float),
        (df["age"] ** 2).rename("age_sq").astype(float),
        reg_dummies,
        df["iscustomer"].astype(float),
    ],
    axis=1,
)

X = X_df.values
Y = df["patents"].values.astype(float)
col_names = list(X_df.columns)
col_names

['intercept',
 'age',

Maximum likelihood estimation with standard errors
We minimize the negative log-likelihood with the analytic gradient (which makes the optimizer fast and stable even with the large age_sq column), then build standard errors from the Hessian. The covariance matrix of the estimates is the inverse of the negative Hessian of the log-likelihood; the standard errors are the square roots of its diagonal.

beta0 = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
fit = optimize.minimize(
    neg_loglik, beta0, args=(Y, X),
    jac=neg_score, method="BFGS"
)
beta_hat = fit.x

# Hessian of the negative log-likelihood for Poisson regression: X' diag(lambda) X
lam_hat = np.exp(np.clip(X @ beta_hat, -30, 30))
hessian = X.T @ (X * lam_hat[:, None])
cov = np.linalg.inv(hessian)
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))

mle_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Coefficient": col_names,
    "Estimate": beta_hat,
    "Std. error": se,
})
show(mle_table, {"Estimate": "{:.4f}", "Std. error": "{:.4f}"},
     "Poisson regression MLE (custom optimizer + Hessian-based SEs)")

Checking against statsmodels GLM
A good sanity check is to fit the identical model with a battle-tested library. If our hand-rolled MLE is correct, the estimates should line up.

    "GLM SE": glm.bse,

The coefficient estimates from our optimizer and from statsmodels are essentially identical — they are solving the same maximization problem, just with different software. The standard errors match very closely as well. Where they differ at all, it is because the two implementations evaluate the curvature of the likelihood slightly differently (our Hessian is computed analytically at the optimum; statsmodels uses its own iteratively-reweighted-least-squares machinery). These are second-order numerical differences, not substantive disagreements.


Interpreting the coefficients
Because the model is multiplicative, a coefficient \(\beta_k\) means that a one-unit increase in \(X_k\) multiplies the expected patent count by \(e^{\beta_k}\), holding everything else fixed.

The age and age-squared coefficients have opposite signs — a positive linear term and a negative quadratic term. Together they describe an inverted-U: expected patenting rises with firm age, but at a decreasing rate, eventually flattening out and turning down for the oldest firms. That is exactly the kind of non-linear life-cycle pattern we suspected, and it justifies having included the quadratic term.
The region coefficients are modest and measured relative to the Midwest baseline; none of them dominates the model. The coefficient that matters most for Blueprinty’s claim is iscustomer, which is positive and sizeable. Exponentiating it implies that, holding age and region fixed, being a Blueprinty customer multiplies a firm’s expected patent count by roughly its exp value above — a meaningful uplift, and one whose standard error is small relative to the estimate. The sign is in the direction the marketing team hoped for, and the magnitude is plausible rather than implausibly large. The next section translates this multiplicative coefficient into something a non-statistician can act on: an average number of additional patents.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software
A coefficient on the log scale is hard to communicate. “Being a customer adds 0.2 to the linear index” means nothing to a marketing executive. Because the model is multiplicative in \(\lambda\), the effect of being a customer is not a fixed number of patents — it depends on each firm’s age and region. The clean way to summarize it is a counterfactual comparison: take every firm exactly as it is, and ask the model what it would predict if that firm were a non-customer versus a customer.

cust_idx = col_names.index("iscustomer")

X0 = X.copy()
X0[:, cust_idx] = 0.0      # everyone treated as a non-customer
X1 = X.copy()
X1[:, cust_idx] = 1.0      # everyone treated as a customer

y0 = np.exp(np.clip(X0 @ beta_hat, -30, 30))
y1 = np.exp(np.clip(X1 @ beta_hat, -30, 30))

diff = y1 - y0
avg_effect = diff.mean()

effect_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": [
        "Avg. predicted patents if non-customer",
        "Avg. predicted patents if customer",
        "Average effect of being a customer",
    ],
    "Value": [y0.mean(), y1.mean(), avg_effect],
})
show(effect_table, {"Value": "{:.3f}"},
     "Counterfactual effect of Blueprinty's software (patents over 5 years)")






Table 8: Counterfactual effect of Blueprinty's software (patents over 5 years)





Quantity
Value




Avg. predicted patents if non-customer
3.436


Avg. predicted patents if customer
4.229


Average effect of being a customer
0.793













Firm-by-firm difference in predicted patents (customer minus non-customer).




Averaging the firm-level differences gives the estimated effect of being a Blueprinty customer, holding each firm’s age and region fixed at its observed values. The model predicts that, on average, a firm awards on the order of 0.4–0.8 additional patents over five years when it uses Blueprinty’s software rather than not. The per-firm histogram shows this effect is positive for essentially every firm, though its size varies because the multiplicative model produces a larger absolute boost for firms that already patent heavily.
A careful conclusion is in order. This analysis does the one thing a raw mean comparison could not: it isolates the customer effect after accounting for the age and regional differences that made customers and non-customers non-comparable to begin with. The estimated effect is positive, statistically precise, and economically meaningful — evidence that is genuinely consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim.
But it is not proof. This is an observational study, not a randomized experiment. Firms chose whether to adopt the software, and that choice may be correlated with characteristics we never observe — managerial quality, R&D intensity, in-house legal expertise — that independently raise patent output. Controlling for age and region removes two confounders; it cannot remove the ones we cannot see. The honest summary is therefore this: the data are consistent with Blueprinty’s software helping firms win more patents, the effect survives the most obvious confounders, but a clean causal claim would require an experiment that this dataset cannot supply.

title: Replicating Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Do minimum wages reduce employment? This is one of the most famous questions in labor economics. Card and Krueger’s 1994 paper studies this question by comparing fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania around New Jersey’s 1992 minimum wage increase. Their empirical strategy is simple and powerful: New Jersey serves as the treated group, Pennsylvania serves as the comparison group, and employment is measured both before and after the policy change. The paper’s headline result is that employment did not fall in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania after the minimum wage increased. In fact, their key difference-in-differences estimate is about 2.76 full-time-equivalent workers. This paper matters because it challenged the standard textbook prediction that raising the minimum wage must reduce employment. Using establishment-level data from 410 restaurants, Card and Krueger instead find no indication that the higher minimum wage reduced employment in this setting.
In this post, I do three things. First, I briefly explain the research design. Second, I replicate the paper’s main difference-in-differences result from Table 3. Third, I extend the analysis by presenting the result visually and estimating a regression version of the same design.

title: Replicating Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Do minimum wages reduce employment? This is one of the most famous questions in labor economics. Card and Krueger’s 1994 paper studies this question by comparing fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania around New Jersey’s 1992 minimum wage increase. Their empirical strategy is simple and powerful: New Jersey serves as the treated group, Pennsylvania serves as the comparison group, and employment is measured both before and after the policy change. The paper’s headline result is that employment did not fall in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania after the minimum wage increased. In fact, their key difference-in-differences estimate is about 2.76 full-time-equivalent workers. This paper matters because it challenged the standard textbook prediction that raising the minimum wage must reduce employment. Using establishment-level data from 410 restaurants, Card and Krueger instead find no indication that the higher minimum wage reduced employment in this setting.
In this post, I do three things. First, I briefly explain the research design. Second, I replicate the paper’s main difference-in-differences result from Table 3. Third, I extend the analysis by presenting the result visually and estimating a regression version of the same design.

title: Replicating Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Research Design
The policy change is straightforward. On April 1, 1992, New Jersey increased its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05, while Pennsylvania did not change its minimum wage at that time. Card and Krueger surveyed fast-food restaurants in both states before and after the increase.
That creates a natural treatment-control setup:

Treatment group: fast-food restaurants in New Jersey
Control group: fast-food restaurants in eastern Pennsylvania
Before period: first-wave survey
After period: second-wave survey

The key outcome is full-time-equivalent employment, or FTE. In the paper, FTE employment is defined as the number of full-time workers plus managers plus one-half the number of part-time workers.
The core estimator is the difference-in-differences:
\[
\text{DID} = (\bar{Y}_{NJ,after} - \bar{Y}_{NJ,before}) - (\bar{Y}_{PA,after} - \bar{Y}_{PA,before})
\]
This compares the change in employment in New Jersey to the change in employment in Pennsylvania, removing broader forces that affect both states.

title: Replicating Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Interpretation
Why was this paper so influential? The answer is that the result goes against the simplest competitive-labor-market prediction. If the textbook model were the full story, a higher minimum wage should reduce employment. Instead, Card and Krueger find no evidence of a negative employment effect in this fast-food setting.
That does not mean minimum wages can never reduce employment in any setting. It does mean that the effect is an empirical question, not something that can be assumed from theory alone. One of the major contributions of this paper is showing how a clean quasi-experimental comparison can challenge a strong prior belief.

title: Replicating Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Conclusion
This replication successfully reproduces the core finding from Card and Krueger (1994). Using the public dataset, I obtain a difference-in-differences estimate of about 2.75 FTE workers, which is nearly identical to the paper’s reported estimate of 2.76.
I also extend the analysis by showing the result graphically and by estimating a regression version of the same design. Across all of these approaches, the conclusion is the same: in this case, the 1992 New Jersey minimum wage increase did not reduce fast-food employment relative to Pennsylvania.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
When someone lands on a website, even a small change in wording can affect whether they take action. Suppose my homepage includes a place where visitors can sign up for a newsletter, and I want to know which message encourages more sign-ups. I will compare two possible calls to action:

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

A standard way to evaluate this kind of design choice is an A/B test. Visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions, and then I compare the sign-up rates across the two groups. Random assignment matters because it helps make the groups comparable, so any systematic difference in outcomes can be attributed to the CTA rather than to differences in the visitors themselves.
In this post, I use a simulated A/B test to explain several core ideas from classical frequentist statistics: the law of large numbers, bootstrap standard errors, the central limit theorem, hypothesis testing, the regression interpretation of a two-sample test, and why “peeking” at results can create misleading findings.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
When someone lands on a website, even a small change in wording can affect whether they take action. Suppose my homepage includes a place where visitors can sign up for a newsletter, and I want to know which message encourages more sign-ups. I will compare two possible calls to action:

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”

A standard way to evaluate this kind of design choice is an A/B test. Visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions, and then I compare the sign-up rates across the two groups. Random assignment matters because it helps make the groups comparable, so any systematic difference in outcomes can be attributed to the CTA rather than to differences in the visitors themselves.
In this post, I use a simulated A/B test to explain several core ideas from classical frequentist statistics: the law of large numbers, bootstrap standard errors, the central limit theorem, hypothesis testing, the regression interpretation of a two-sample test, and why “peeking” at results can create misleading findings.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor either signs up or does not sign up, so each individual outcome can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable. If a visitor sees CTA A, their sign-up probability is \(\pi_A\). If a visitor sees CTA B, their sign-up probability is \(\pi_B\).
That means each observation is either:

\(1\) if the visitor signs up
\(0\) if the visitor does not sign up

The parameter I care about is the difference in sign-up rates:
\[
\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B
\]
If \(\theta > 0\), CTA A performs better. If \(\theta < 0\), CTA B performs better. If \(\theta = 0\), the two CTAs perform equally well.
A natural estimator for this quantity is the difference in sample means:
\[
\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B
\]
Because the data are binary, each sample mean is just a sample proportion. So \(\bar{X}_A = \hat{\pi}_A\) and \(\bar{X}_B = \hat{\pi}_B\).

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real A/B test, we would not know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\). We would only observe data and try to infer the underlying sign-up rates. For this exercise, though, it is useful to set the truth ourselves so that we can study how our estimator behaves when we know the answer in advance.
I will assume:

\(\pi_A = 0.22\)
\(\pi_B = 0.18\)

So the true difference is:
\[
\theta = 0.22 - 0.18 = 0.04
\]
The next chunk simulates 1,000 visitors in each group.

n_A = 1000
n_B = 1000
pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
theta_true = pi_A - pi_B

A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n_A)
B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n_B)

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "group": ["A"] * n_A + ["B"] * n_B,
    "signup": np.concatenate([A, B])
})

summary_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Group": ["A", "B"],
    "Sample size": [n_A, n_B],
    "True signup rate": [pi_A, pi_B],
    "Observed signup rate": [A.mean(), B.mean()]
})

summary_table["True signup rate"] = summary_table["True signup rate"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.3f}")
summary_table["Observed signup rate"] = summary_table["Observed signup rate"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.3f}")

Even though the true rates are 0.22 and 0.18, the observed proportions in any one sample will usually not match those values exactly. That sampling variation is the main reason statistical inference is necessary.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) says that as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the population mean. In this setting, that means the average outcome in group A should get closer to \(\pi_A\), the average outcome in group B should get closer to \(\pi_B\), and therefore the difference in sample means \(\hat{\theta}\) should get closer to the true difference \(\theta\) as we collect more data.
To make this concrete, I compute the element-wise differences between the simulated A and B outcomes, then track the cumulative average of those differences.

diffs = A - B
running_mean = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, len(diffs) + 1)






Running average of the difference in outcomes between CTA A and CTA B.




At the beginning of the sample, the cumulative average jumps around a lot because each new observation has a large influence on the overall mean. As more observations accumulate, those random fluctuations become less important and the running mean settles down near the true value of 0.04. That is the practical value of the law of large numbers: it explains why larger experiments produce more stable estimates.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Once we have a point estimate, the next question is how much uncertainty surrounds it. A point estimate alone does not tell us whether the observed difference is precise or noisy.
One flexible way to measure precision is the bootstrap. The idea is simple: repeatedly resample with replacement from the observed data, recompute the statistic on each resample, and use the spread of those resampled statistics to estimate the standard error.
Here I generate 1,000 bootstrap resamples for each group and compute a bootstrapped estimate of \(\theta\) for each one.

theta_hat = A.mean() - B.mean()

n_boot = 1000
boot_thetas = np.empty(n_boot)

for i in range(n_boot):
    A_star = np.random.choice(A, size=n_A, replace=True)
    B_star = np.random.choice(B, size=n_B, replace=True)
    boot_thetas[i] = A_star.mean() - B_star.mean()

boot_se = boot_thetas.std(ddof=1)

pi_hat_A = A.mean()
pi_hat_B = B.mean()

analytic_se = np.sqrt(
    pi_hat_A * (1 - pi_hat_A) / n_A +
    pi_hat_B * (1 - pi_hat_B) / n_B
)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * boot_se
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * boot_se

bootstrap_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": [
        "Estimated difference (theta_hat)",
        "Bootstrap standard error",
        "Analytical standard error",
        "95% CI lower bound",
        "95% CI upper bound"
    ],
    "Value": [theta_hat, boot_se, analytic_se, ci_lower, ci_upper]
})

bootstrap_results["Value"] = bootstrap_results["Value"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.4f}")

The bootstrap standard error and the analytical standard error should be very close, and in this simulation they usually are. That is reassuring because it tells us that the resampling approach is capturing the same uncertainty that the closed-form Bernoulli formula does.
Using the bootstrap standard error, I construct a 95% confidence interval as \(\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times SE_{boot}\). Interpreted informally, this interval gives a plausible range of values for the true difference in sign-up rates. If the interval excludes zero, that suggests the data are more consistent with a real CTA effect than with no difference at all.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says that, under broad conditions, the sampling distribution of a sample mean becomes approximately Normal as the sample size grows. Because my estimator is the difference of two sample means, the same idea applies here: even though the underlying data are Bernoulli rather than Normal, the distribution of \(\hat{\theta}\) becomes increasingly bell-shaped when the sample size is large.
To illustrate that, I simulate the estimator 1,000 times at four different sample sizes.

sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
clt_results = {}

for n in sample_sizes:
    estimates = np.empty(1000)
    for i in range(1000):
        A_n = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
        B_n = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n)
        estimates[i] = A_n.mean() - B_n.mean()
    clt_results[n] = estimates






Sampling distribution of the difference in sample means at different sample sizes.




With only 25 observations per group, the histogram is still fairly rough and discrete-looking. By the time the sample size reaches 100 or 500 per group, the distribution is much smoother and more symmetric. This is exactly the pattern predicted by the CLT. The theorem is important because it justifies using Normal-based confidence intervals and hypothesis tests in large samples, even when the raw data are binary.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
A hypothesis test starts by specifying a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis. Here the natural null is:
\[
H_0: \theta = 0
\]
which says that the two CTAs have the same sign-up rate. The alternative is:
\[
H_1: \theta \neq 0
\]
which says that the CTAs differ.
To test this, I standardize the observed estimate:
\[
z = \frac{\hat{\theta} - 0}{SE(\hat{\theta})}
\]
Why do this? Because the CLT tells us that for large samples, \(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately Normal. Under the null, its mean is 0. Dividing by its standard error puts the statistic onto the standard Normal scale. Once that is done, I can compute a p-value using the familiar \(N(0,1)\) distribution.
This is often loosely called a “t-test,” but that label is not quite exact here. The classical t-test comes from Normal data with an estimated variance, which produces an exact t-distribution. In this setting, the observations are Bernoulli rather than Normal, so the CLT gives us only an approximate Normal result. In large samples, though, the standard Normal and the t-distribution are so similar that the practical difference is usually small.

z_stat = theta_hat / analytic_se
p_value = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z_stat)))

hypothesis_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Statistic": ["Estimated difference", "Standard error", "z statistic", "Two-sided p-value"],
    "Value": [theta_hat, analytic_se, z_stat, p_value]
})

hypothesis_results["Value"] = hypothesis_results["Value"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.4f}")

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
The same comparison can also be written as a regression. Stack the observations into one dataset and define:

\(Y_i = 1\) if visitor \(i\) signs up, and \(0\) otherwise
\(D_i = 1\) if visitor \(i\) sees CTA A, and \(0\) if visitor \(i\) sees CTA B

Then fit:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]
This regression has a very intuitive interpretation:

\(\beta_0\) is the mean of group B, so it estimates \(\pi_B\)
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1\) is the mean of group A, so it estimates \(\pi_A\)
Therefore \(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\)

So the coefficient on the treatment indicator should match the difference in sample means from the earlier sections.

df_reg = df.copy()
df_reg["D"] = (df_reg["group"] == "A").astype(int)

X = sm.add_constant(df_reg["D"])
model = sm.OLS(df_reg["signup"], X).fit()

beta1 = model.params["D"]
beta1_se = model.bse["D"]
beta1_t = model.tvalues["D"]
beta1_p = model.pvalues["D"]

regression_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["beta_1 estimate", "Standard error", "t statistic", "p-value"],
    "Regression": [beta1, beta1_se, beta1_t, beta1_p],
    "Two-sample approach": [theta_hat, analytic_se, z_stat, p_value]
})

regression_results["Regression"] = regression_results["Regression"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.4f}")
regression_results["Two-sample approach"] = regression_results["Two-sample approach"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.4f}")

This equivalence matters because it shows that regression is not a completely different tool. In simple experiments, it is just another way to express the same comparison. More importantly, regression scales naturally: if I want to add controls, interactions, or multiple treatment arms later, I can do so within the same framework.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
Now suppose my boss is impatient and wants to peek at the results every time another 100 visitors per group have been observed. That means testing after 100, 200, 300, …, up to 1,000 observations per group. If any one of those tests is significant at the 0.05 level, she wants to stop early and declare a winner.
This is a problem under classical frequentist inference. A single hypothesis test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% chance of a false positive when the null is true. But repeated looks at accumulating data create repeated opportunities to get “lucky” noise. The overall probability of seeing at least one statistically significant result becomes much larger than 5%.
To show that, I simulate a world where the null is true: \(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\).

np.random.seed(496)

n_total = 1000
peek_points = np.arange(100, 1001, 100)
n_experiments = 10000
pi_null = 0.20

any_sig = np.zeros(n_experiments, dtype=bool)

for exp in range(n_experiments):
    A_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)
    B_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)

    sig_found = False

    for n in peek_points:
        A_n = A_null[:n]
        B_n = B_null[:n]

        theta_n = A_n.mean() - B_n.mean()
        se_n = np.sqrt(
            A_n.mean() * (1 - A_n.mean()) / n +
            B_n.mean() * (1 - B_n.mean()) / n
        )

        if se_n == 0:
            continue

        z_n = theta_n / se_n
        p_n = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z_n)))

        if p_n < 0.05:
            sig_found = True
            break

    any_sig[exp] = sig_found

false_positive_rate = any_sig.mean()

peeking_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Procedure": ["Single test at n = 1000", "Peeking every 100 observations"],
    "False positive rate": [0.05, false_positive_rate]
})

peeking_results["False positive rate"] = peeking_results["False positive rate"].map(lambda x: f"{x:.4f}")
peeking_results








Procedure

False positive rate under a single test versus repeated peeking.




The simulation usually shows that the false positive rate under repeated peeking is much larger than 0.05. In other words, if I repeatedly check the data and stop whenever I happen to cross the significance threshold, I dramatically increase my chance of falsely declaring a winner.
That is why A/B tests need a pre-specified stopping rule or a formal sequential testing procedure. Without one, “significance” can become a product of impatience rather than evidence.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Conclusion
This A/B testing example ties together several foundational ideas in frequentist statistics.

The Law of Large Numbers explains why the difference in sample means stabilizes as the experiment grows.
The bootstrap provides a practical way to estimate uncertainty.
The Central Limit Theorem justifies Normal-based inference for large samples.
Hypothesis testing turns the estimate into a formal decision rule.
The same comparison can be expressed as a regression, showing how experimental analysis fits into a broader modeling framework.
Finally, peeking demonstrates that statistical procedures depend not just on formulas, but also on disciplined experimental design.

Even in a simple A/B test, the language of classical statistics gives us a rigorous way to reason about evidence, uncertainty, and decision-making.
